subject: Chemistry
title: The Maillard Reaction: Why Food Browns
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Maillard Reaction: Why Food Browns usable.

hook.text: That golden crust on toast, seared steak, and roasted coffee all come from the same chemical reaction.

buildup.text: When sugars and amino acids are heated above 140°C, they react to create hundreds of new flavor compounds.

discovery.text: Louis-Camille Maillard described this in 1912. It's not caramelization—it requires both sugar and protein.

twist.text: The reaction produces over 1,000 different molecules. That's why cooked food is so much more complex than raw.

climax.text: Chefs manipulate it by controlling heat, pH, and moisture. The Maillard reaction is cooking's secret weapon.

punchline.text: Sugar plus protein plus heat. That's the flavor of cooking.

quiz.question: What two ingredients does the Maillard reaction require?

details.summary: The Maillard reaction is a complex chemical process between amino acids and reducing sugars that occurs when food is heated above 140 degrees Celsius..
details.whyItMatters: The Maillard reaction is responsible for the flavors of bread crusts, grilled meat, roasted coffee, and toasted marshmallows. It is arguably the most important chemical reaction in cooking.
takeaways: Amino acids react with sugars at temperatures above 140 degrees Celsius
The reaction produces hundreds of unique flavor and aroma compounds
It is different from caramelization, which involves only sugars

faq.question: Why does boiled food not develop the same flavors as roasted or grilled food?
faq.answer: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius, below the 140 degrees needed for the Maillard reaction. The water on the food surface keeps the temperature at 100 degrees until it evaporates. This is why searing meat at high heat creates a flavorful crust while boiling does not.

faq.question: What is the difference between the Maillard reaction and caramelization?
faq.answer: Caramelization involves only sugars heated above about 170 degrees Celsius, while the Maillard reaction requires both amino acids and sugars. The Maillard reaction starts at lower temperatures and produces more complex flavor compounds because proteins contribute nitrogen-containing molecules.
